newsitem.title: USA: Consumers prices inch up slightly in July.
newsitem.headline: Consumers prices inch up slightly in July.

text.p: Consumer prices registered a modest increase last month, the government said Thursday in another report showing that inflation remains well under control.

As expected, the Labor Department's Consumer Price Index edged up 0.2 percent in July after rising 0.1 percent in June. The so-called "core" rate of inflation, which leaves out the often erratic food and energy measures, also rose 0.2 percent.
The small increase in the overall index and the closely watched core rate matched Wall Street expectations.

"What we have here is a very low inflation rate," said Philip Braverman, an economist at DKB Securities. "Yesterday's (Producer Price Index) report showed outright deflation in the pipeline and now we have a confirmation that in the consumer prices we continue to see very subdued inflation."
A drop of 0.1 percent in energy prices had a moderating effect on the overall price gains and may surprise some analysts who had predicted that component of the index would show a gain in July.

July food prices rose 0.3 percent, while grocery store prices also rose 0.3 percent, reflecting larger increases in the indexes for meats, poultry, fish, and other key food categories, the department said.
Apparel prices, up 0.2 percent, and transportation prices, which rose 0.1 percent in July, staged a rebound from June, when both areas had posted declines.
Analysts had expected the report to show few signs of inflation, saying that businesses have been reluctant to push up prices despite mounting evidence of consumer confidence and plentiful jobs.
The Producer Price Index released on Wednesday showed wholesale prices falling for a record seventh consecutive month.
In another report, the Commerce Department said inventories held by businesses took their biggest jump in more than two years in June, mostly because of a bulge in unsold goods held by wholesalers.
A separate report issued by the Labor Department showed the number of Americans claiming first-time jobless benefits in the week ended Aug. 9 rose by 12,000 to 316,000.

The four-week moving average of claims, which economists say provides a better gauge of labor market trends than the more-volatile weekly number, fell to 298,250. That was its lowest level since the week ended Feb. 11, 1989, when claims stood at 297,750.
The inflation-sensitive 30-year U.S. Treasury bond gained a third of a point on the reports, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, fell to 6.60 percent from 6.63 percent on Wednesday.
